newsitem.title: INDIA: Nearly 70 pct of US investment headed for W. India. [CORRECTED 11:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Nearly 70 pct of US investment headed for W. India. [CORRECTED 11:40 GMT]

text.p: India's industrialised western region is expected to attract $3.3 billion of American investment over the four years to 2001, accounting for 67 percent of the total for the country, U.S. Ambassador Frank Wisner said on Friday. (Corrects to make clear the $3.3 billion is 67 percent of the total investment).
Wisner told a meeting of businessmen that Indian economic reforms had achieved a lot, but their complete potential could only be realised by determined implementation of policies.

"Our projections show that of the over $5,000 million of new investment expected from 1997 to 2001, western India will have the lion's share -- $3,369 million, or 67 percent of the total," Wisner told the Indo-American Chamber of Commerce.
Wisner said the figure had been generated by a recent U.S. embassy study of American investment patterns in India.
He said the country's wealthiest state of Maharashtra had attracted between 30 and 45 percent of total US investment in India despite its numerous lengthy bureaucratic procedures.
"Of total U.S. investment in India of $1,339 million in India until the end of 1995, Maharashtra alone had captured $605 million, or 45.2 percent of the total," Wisner said.
He said the figure for western India -- including states besides Maharashtra -- had dropped slightly in 1996, to 32 percent, or $135 million of the total of $425 million invested.

"The problem most often cited for Maharashtra was red tape, an incredible volume and variety of red tape," Wisner said, warning the businessmen that investors would choose to put their money in those states where it would bring results fastest.
He said two recent steps by India had given proof of the country's determination to revitalise its economy.
"India's most recent budget was welcome evidence of a national determination to build an economy based on modern, free-market principles, and to engage further global markets," Wisner said.
"So, too, was India's recent decision in the World Trade Organisation to sign the Information Technology Agreement."
Wisner called for India to give up the balance of payments protection it has enjoyed for more than 40 years under GATT.

"At the end of this month, India will have yet another opportunity to signal its willingness to participate as a full partner in the world trading system by setting aside the balance of payments protection," he said.
"This is a step that would be welcomed by all of India's trading partners," Wisner added.
